canonical_statement: The study aimed to assess the safety of fixed-dose heparin titration boluses in underweight patients (BMI <18.5 kg/m²) compared with patients with BMI 18.5–29.9 kg/m².
UNC used a nurse-driven adult thrombosis nomogram based on heparin correlation values (HCVs), with 5,000-unit fixed-dose titration boluses for subtherapeutic HCVs.

canonical_statement: This was a retrospective, single-center electronic medical record review of patients treated with unfractionated heparin for VTE from April 2014 through July 2022.
Patients were eligible if they were at least 18 years old and received at least one heparin titration bolus under the institutional adult thrombosis nomogram.

inclusion_criteria: Received at least one titration bolus per the institutional adult thrombosis nomogram

canonical_statement: Exclusion criteria were pregnancy, incarceration, BMI ≥30 kg/m², heparin discontinuation before the first HCV was collected, or a pre-admission acquired/hereditary coagulopathy identified by specified ICD codes.

canonical_statement: Because the control pool was much larger, controls were randomly selected 1:1 to the underweight group; only the first qualifying heparin encounter per patient was analyzed.
The primary outcome was the percentage of patients with a supratherapeutic HCV after the first heparin titration bolus.

concept.text: Supratherapeutic HCV after first titration bolus

outcome.definition: HCV above the nomogram therapeutic range after the first titration bolus.

canonical_statement: Stable HCV was defined as two consecutive HCVs in the therapeutic range drawn at least 6 hours apart.

outcome.definition: Two consecutive HCVs within the therapeutic range, drawn at least 6 hours apart.

canonical_statement: Clinically significant bleeding required a hemoglobin decrease ≥2 g/dL within 24 hours plus at least one of: ≥2 units packed red blood cells within 24 hours, protamine administration, imaging-documented organ bleeding, or fatal bleeding.

outcome.definition: Hemoglobin decrease ≥2 g/dL within 24 hours plus ≥2 units PRBC within 24 hours, protamine, imaging-documented organ bleeding, or fatal bleed.

canonical_statement: Categorical comparisons used Pearson chi-square tests; parametric continuous comparisons used independent-samples t tests; nonparametric continuous comparisons used Mann–Whitney U tests; p<0.05 was considered statistically significant.
The study screened 1,115 patients: 101 in the BMI <18.5 kg/m² pool and 1,014 in the BMI 18.5–29.9 kg/m² pool.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that there was no statistically significant difference in supratherapeutic HCV after the first titration bolus between BMI groups and observed no clinically significant bleeding in either group.

The authors considered the more frequent heparin holds in underweight patients, together with their significantly higher titration-bolus dose per kilogram, a safety concern for current heparin management.
The authors proposed that large titration boluses may overcorrect subtherapeutic HCVs, prompt infusion pauses, and thereby delay stable therapeutic anticoagulation.
The study did not assess HCV trends associated with every bolus across each patient’s full treatment course because of limitations and potential confounding factors.
Use of HCV rather than conventional aPTT monitoring may limit comparison and generalizability to other centers.
Defining underweight by BMI rather than a weight cutoff may limit comparability with similar studies.
The underweight group had a wide range of total body weights; the authors noted that restricting inclusion to patients under 50 kg might have improved comparison with prior studies.
The relatively small sample size may have limited the ability to detect a significant difference between groups.

Although the primary outcome did not differ between groups, the authors remained concerned that underweight patients may be at increased risk of over-anticoagulation and called for further studies of fixed-dose titration bolus safety.
The study reported no specific funding from public, commercial, or not-for-profit agencies.
The authors declared no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work.
